evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 形義通解 / graphic formation and usage
evidence.text: The database interprets oracle-bone and bronze 干 as a shield, reportedly with feather decoration, and says its protective sense developed from the defensive object. It cites an oracle-bone example from 合集 28059, 弜令戍干衛, glossed as defensive/protective use; a bronze-vessel example 豦簋「干戈」 uses it for the weapon. It also records the *Book of Documents*, “稱爾戈，比爾干，立爾矛,” with the traditional commentary glossing 干 as a shield. The database reports a competing proposal by Xu Zhongshu that oracle-bone 干 and 單 are variant forms representing a forked hunting implement. These are source interpretations; I did not inspect the glyph images.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 干

evidence.source: CASE Press / National Taiwan University science communication
evidence.text: The author argues that the earliest forms proposed for 干 are Shang oracle-bone signs, with earlier and later Shang shapes differing in a way interpreted as reflecting shield-decoration change. The article says 干 is securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription on the 豦簋, shaped like a round shield with a forked top; a related shape occurs on the late-Western Zhou 毛公鼎. By later Western Zhou the upper round feature is written as a short horizontal stroke, and this form continues through Spring-and-Autumn and Warring States scripts, small seal, Qin clerical and Western Han clerical forms; the forked top is regularized to a shorter horizontal stroke by Eastern Han. The article’s earliest Shang identification is presented as a proposal, while the mid-Western Zhou 豦簋 attestation is stated as the secure point. It reports disagreement on whether certain Shang signs should be read 干, 盾, or another graph.
evidence.title: 商周時期的防護裝具與兵器：甲、冑、干、盾（四）

evidence.source: 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.field: Western Zhou bronze readings / disputed graph identification
evidence.text: Su Jianzhou reviews competing readings of Western Zhou bronze signs: scholars including Luo Zhenyu, Zhu Fangpu and Yu Shengwu identify a shield pictograph; Guo Moruo’s views changed, and Lin Yun distinguishes 干 from 盾 in some forms. Su argues from paired inscription contexts, including 豦簋 “介胄干戈,” that related forms are 干. This supports that the shield reading has substantial scholarly backing, while showing that particular bronze shapes and distinctions from 盾 have been disputed. The article dates its publication to 2017-02-12.
evidence.title: 蘇建洲：西周金文“干”字再議

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The database quotes Shuowen: 干, 犯也。从反入，从一. This is Xu Shen’s Han-period explanation (“to offend/violate,” analyzed as 反入 plus 一), not independent confirmation of the shield picture. The database separately reports oracle-bone defensive use and bronze examples meaning shield, showing that graphic origin and Shuowen’s semantic analysis should not be conflated.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 干

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: For 干, the database gives Guangyun 古寒切 and Middle Chinese category 見母, level tone, 寒 rhyme, open division, first grade. This is the shield graph’s historical pronunciation evidence; no component is proposed as a phonetic element in this simple graph. Its page gives modern reading material but the actual Mandarin symbols are embedded as images in the opened text, so this research record does not claim a complete modern-reading citation from that page.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 干

evidence.source: Kotobank, 普及版 字通 entry
evidence.text: The entry treats 干 as a pictograph of a rectangular shield and gives senses including shield, defend/protect, offend, concern/participate, and uses in which it is interchangeable with 乾 or 幹. It cites the 毛公鼎 phrase 干吾王身 as a protective/defensive use. This is a dictionary’s interpretation, not a direct paleographic inspection here.
evidence.title: 干(カン)とは？ 意味や使い方 — コトバンク / 普及版 字通

evidence.field: 乾 formation, readings, senses, dated textual examples
evidence.text: The Ministry dictionary records 乾 as a distinct traditional graph, with 干 among its variants and 干 as its simplified correspondence. It quotes Shuowen’s “上出也。从乙；乙，物之達也。倝聲” and identifies 倝 as the sound element and 乙 as semantic. It records modern Mandarin qián for the ‘emerge upward/heaven/yang’ reading and gān for ‘dry’; it cites the *Book of Odes*, 王風·中谷有蓷, “中谷有蓷，暵其乾矣,” for the dry sense, and the *Zuo zhuan* (僖公十五年) and *Shan Hai Jing* for parched/dried-up senses. This separates the dry word and the cosmological/heavenly use; the source gives no date for when the dry reading began.
evidence.title: A00044 乾 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 乾 sound component and historical pronunciation
evidence.text: The database quotes Shuowen’s analysis of 乾 as from 乙 with 倝 as sound. It records two Guangyun fanqie readings, 古寒 and 渠焉, and classifies them respectively as 見母 level 寒 rhyme and 群母 level 仙 rhyme, open division. These distinct historical reading categories correspond to the dry and qián/heaven reading split in the dictionary’s entry. The evidence supports 倝 as the source’s proposed phonetic element, but this research did not independently inspect 倝’s original depicted referent.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 乾

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The database describes 幹 as also written 干 and gives early textual examples for ‘main stem/trunk’: *Liji*, 月令, 羽箭幹; *Zuo zhuan*, 昭公二十五年, 幹 for the body’s frame/bones; and *Yi*, 乾卦, “貞者，事之幹也,” extended metaphorically to the basis or mainstay of affairs. It also records later ‘ability,’ ‘manage/take charge,’ and ‘business/matter’ senses with citations from *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, *Han shu*, and Song writings. Its entry supplies Guangyun 古案切 and Middle Chinese 見母 level/去-tone-category data; this is separate from the original shield graph and does not make 干 a component in 幹 a sound element.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 幹

gaps: No sound-component role is proposed for the target graph 干 itself; the shield interpretation is pictographic, not phonetic.

The physical oracle-bone and bronze glyph images were not visually inspected. The article reports competing readings and uncertainty over some Shang forms; secure 干 attestation is stated by the CASE article as mid-Western Zhou 豦簋.

The pictorial referent is disputed: the leading interpretation is a shield; a minority account treats some oracle-bone forms as a variant of 單 depicting a forked hunting implement. The object’s name/pronunciation is not independently recovered here, but no whole-graph phonetic-loan claim for a weapon-name is needed to explain 干.

乾’s dry word and qián/heaven word have separate dictionary readings and fanqie categories, but the sources inspected do not establish a precise chronology or the semantic bridge between them. The dry sense is attested in the *Book of Odes*; the source provides no date for the reading’s first use.

幹’s cited textual history establishes trunk/mainstay and later extensions, but no evidence inspected establishes that its graph is historically derived from 干 or that 干 inside 幹 has a semantic or phonetic role. Modern simplified correspondence is a spelling policy, not proof of a shared ancient graphic origin.

The record’s modern readings include Mandarin gàn, Cantonese gon1, and Japanese kan readings, but no component-level sound comparison applies to 干. Full historical reconstructions for 干 and 倝 were not independently established by the opened sources; only Guangyun categories/fanqie were checked.
Some search-result URLs were not accessible on open; no claim above relies on uninspected page content beyond the specifically labeled search-result record.
